clue.text: Casseroles, say, old and new, Vera smashed

indicators.note: something smashed is broken into bits, so the letters are reassembled in a fresh order

parts.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Vera has dropped her casserole dishes, old and new alike, and broken the lot.
explanation.walkthrough: The dishes Vera smashed are, fittingly, what the answer names. 'Casseroles, say' is a definition by example: the 'say' warns that casseroles are one kind of the thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Casserole dishes are one example of the heatproof cooking vessels made to go inside a kitchen stove.

clue.text: More than likely to give you a good run for your money?

definitions.text: More than likely to give you a good run for your money?

parts.note: the surface: something is very probable, as in an everyday expression of confidence

parts.words: to give you a good run for your money
parts.note: the setter's reading: a racehorse whose price is shorter than evens, the favourite a punter backs to run well

explanation.walkthrough: 'A good run for your money' is an idiom for fair value, but here it is literal: the horse you bet on runs well. In betting, a price shorter than evens means the bookmaker rates a win as more likely than not.
explanation.definitionFit: A favourite priced shorter than evens is expected to win, so the phrase describes any outcome judged more probable than not.

clue.text: Blue celestial body close to Mercury

parts.note: our planet is a body in the heavens

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the planet's name

explanation.surface: An astronomy note: a blue planet lying near Mercury in the solar system.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'blue celestial body' as the blue planet, but 'Blue' stands alone as the definition in its sense of rude or smutty. 'Close to' looks like 'near' but means the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue jokes are coarse or smutty ones, and crude, bawdy humour is also described with this adjective.

clue.text: Endless battle to secure first couple of points in game

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is cut off
to secure something is to hold it fast, so one piece is placed inside another

parts.note: the Battle of Waterloo, 1815, with its last letter dropped

indicators.note: the first two letters of the word that follows are the only ones kept

parts.note: the opening pair of letters of the word

explanation.surface: A tense match in which a side battles to win its first couple of points.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Points' looks like the score of the game, but it only supplies its first two letters. Waterloo is the battle where Wellington defeated Napoleon.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a team sport played by swimmers in a pool, who try to throw a ball into the opposing goal.

clue.text: Style of popular music? Butler had hymns playing

indicators.note: things that are playing are in motion and messing about, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the three words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A butler with hymns playing on the stereo prompts the question of what kind of music this is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing' fits the music surface so snugly that it hardly looks like a signal; all fourteen letters of the three words are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a genre of African American popular music from the 1940s onward, blending jazz, gospel and blues.

clue.text: Weak shell of elegant mollusc

parts.note: limp means feeble or lacking strength

indicators.note: a shell is the outer casing, so only the outside letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A naturalist's note: a graceful sea creature with a fragile shell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shell' belongs so naturally with 'mollusc' that it reads as the creature's shell, not as a signal to take the outer letters of 'elegant'.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a sea snail with a conical shell that clings tightly to rocks, a kind of marine gastropod.

clue.text: Likeness, as Father Time might say

parts.note: someone introducing himself would begin 'I'm'
the old man with scythe and hourglass personifies passing time, and so age

explanation.surface: A likeness that old Father Time might speak of.
explanation.walkthrough: Father Time is the bearded old figure with scythe and hourglass; if he announced who he was, 'I'm age' run together makes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A picture or statue showing someone is a representation or portrait of them, so a copy of their appearance.

clue.text: Picked up tonic, one for a woman

indicators.note: to pick up words is to hear them, so what counts is how they sound

parts.note: a fillip is a tonic or boost, and one is A

explanation.surface: Someone picks up a tonic water, one of them meant for a woman at the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tonic' suggests a drink, but here it is a fillip, a stimulus that perks you up. Said together, 'fillip, a' sounds like the girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a female first name, the feminine form of Philip, so it names one particular woman.

clue.text: Continuously move up bound by rope?

indicators.note: something bound by another is tied inside it, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: a tether is a rope that ties an animal

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top, so backwards

parts.note: to move is to go

explanation.surface: A climber keeps moving up a rock face, roped in all the while.
explanation.walkthrough: The climbing picture makes 'move up bound by rope' look like one action, but it splits into a reversed piece held inside a rope.
explanation.definitionFit: As in 'for hours together', the word means without a break, in unbroken sequence.

clue.text: Film taking hour, for example, about a supermarket nearly breaking record

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the last letter goes
breaking into something means getting inside it, so a group is placed within

parts.note: to tape something is to record it
H is the abbreviation for hour
e.g. is the Latin abbreviation
re means concerning
taken as written
Tesco, the British supermarket chain, missing its final letter

explanation.surface: A documentary about a supermarket that is close to setting a record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like it wraps something, but it is simply RE. Tesco is Britain's largest supermarket chain. The 1963 war film follows prisoners breaking out of a German camp.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the title of the 1963 Second World War movie starring Steve McQueen, a single cinema release.

clue.text: Girl crashed hot rod approaching end of motorway

indicators.note: a crashed vehicle is wrecked and bent out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, the only one kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A young woman wrecks her souped-up car as she nears the end of the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: A hot rod is a car modified for speed, so 'crashed' fits the driving scene while quietly signalling the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a female first name, so any girl so called fits; crosswords often define names this way.

clue.text: Catching a chance to speak

definitions.meaning: first meaning: perceiving a sound, as in catching what someone said
second meaning: an opportunity to state one's case

explanation.walkthrough: 'Catching' suggests infection or grabbing, but here it means picking up sound with the ears.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both the present participle of perceiving sounds and a noun for an opportunity to present your side.

clue.text: To back her — that's different

indicators.note: going back means travelling the opposite way, so the letters run right to left

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Supporting her would be a change of stance, a departure from the usual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To back her' reads as 'to support her', but 'back' only turns round the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Other means not the same one, distinct or alternative, which is what different means.

clue.text: Call for attention, receiving variable information about one health expert

indicators.note: whatever receives something takes it in, so the outer piece holds the rest

parts.note: 'hist!' is an old exclamation to attract notice, like 'psst'
Y is a standard algebraic variable

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one piece goes round another

parts.note: gen is British slang for information
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone calls for attention after receiving news about a health expert.
explanation.walkthrough: Gen, British slang for the facts, goes round I; Y joins it and the pair sit inside the old hushing call 'hist'.
explanation.definitionFit: A hygienist is a specialist in cleanliness and disease prevention, notably a dental one who cleans teeth.

clue.text: In which Sun has special role diminished?

definitions.text: In which Sun has special role diminished?

indicators.note: something diminished is reduced from its proper form, so the letters lose their original order

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for Sunday
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A riddle asking for the event in which our star's usual starring part is cut down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sun' means the star in the surface but gives only S, the abbreviation for Sunday. The whole clue is also the definition: during this event the sun's light is cut off.
explanation.definitionFit: When the moon passes in front of it, the daytime star is darkened, so its role of lighting the earth is reduced.

clue.text: Appear behind guard

parts.note: to look a certain way is to appear so
behind in order or time means after

explanation.walkthrough: 'Appear behind' reads as one phrase, like a guard who emerges at your back, but it is two words each giving a piece.
explanation.definitionFit: To guard someone is to protect and keep watch over them, which is to take care of them.

clue.text: Primarily, spiky annual notoriously distributing seedcases. Painful underfoot? Rather!

definitions.text: Primarily, spiky annual notoriously distributing seedcases. Painful underfoot? Rather!

indicators.note: primarily means in the first place, so each word gives its opening letter

parts.words: spiky annual notoriously distributing seedcases. Painful underfoot? Rather
parts.note: the initial letters of the eight words in sequence

explanation.surface: A botanical description of a prickly yearly plant whose spiny seed pods hurt to tread on.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue both describes the plant and spells it: the plant is a grass whose burs are notorious for stabbing bare feet.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an American grass, genus Cenchrus, whose spiny burs spread its seed and prick anyone walking barefoot.

clue.text: Proper mixture of Brie and meat

parts.note: prim means stiffly proper and correct

indicators.note: a mixture is things stirred together, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A recipe for a proper blend of soft cheese and meat.
explanation.walkthrough: The cheese is only there for its letters; 'Proper' suggests correct, and prim is a fussily correct kind of proper.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a premium roast beef cut from the rib section of the animal, so a kind of butcher's joint.

clue.text: Cool, American, ironic? 'Not I!', troubled Democrat's interrupting

parts.note: A is a standard abbreviation for American

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break in on something, so a piece goes inside another
something troubled is disturbed and agitated, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the three words taken letter for letter
D stands for Democrat in US politics

explanation.surface: A cool, ironic American denies everything while a worried Democrat keeps butting in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cool' sits among 'American, ironic' like one more adjective describing a person, but it is the definition, a verb. The 's' after Democrat is short for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: To cool a room or building by mechanical refrigeration of the air is to fit or run such a system.

clue.text: Bill will have to call back for this kind of acid

parts.note: AC is short for account, a bill

indicators.note: going back means travelling the opposite way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: to cite someone is to summon them to court

explanation.surface: Bill will have to phone back to ask about a particular acid.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill looks like a man's name who must return a call, but it is an account; 'call back' is a reversed summons.
explanation.definitionFit: Acetic acid is the sharp compound that gives vinegar its sour taste, so the adjective names that type.

clue.text: Good man, having acquired skills, sets forth

parts.note: a saint is a good man, abbreviated ST
arts are skills, as in the arts of war

explanation.surface: A good man, now properly trained, sets out on his journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good man' for a saint is a crossword staple; skills as arts is the older sense of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: To set forth is to begin a journey or begin something, and to start is to begin.

clue.text: Homes, easy to manage, son: about half a mile

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps around another

parts.note: docile means compliant and easily controlled

indicators.note: half a word is one of its two halves, here the first two letters

parts.note: a first letter selection: half the word, its first two of four letters
S is the standard abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: An estate agent's pitch: easy-to-run houses, son, about half a mile off.
explanation.walkthrough: The agent's listing implies distance; really half of 'mile' goes inside the word for manageable, with S after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A domicile is a formal or legal word for the place where someone lives permanently.

clue.text: Pass fashionable man

parts.note: a col is a mountain pass
in means in fashion

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass' looks like a verb, as in walking past a stylish man, but it is a noun: a col is a low gap between mountain peaks.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a common male first name, so it fits any man bearing it, a regular crossword convention.

clue.text: A Highlander in a cravat

parts.note: taken as written
a Highlander comes from the Scottish Highlands

explanation.surface: A Scotsman from the hills dressed up in a neck scarf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' reads as a container signal, but it merely links wordplay to definition: a Scot is a cravat.
explanation.definitionFit: An ascot is a broad neck scarf worn looped under the chin, a type of formal neckwear.

clue.text: Exercises including a part for one released from prison

indicators.note: to include something is to have it inside, so one piece holds another

parts.note: PE is physical education, school exercises
taken as written
a part in a play is a role

explanation.surface: Prison drama classes give an inmate on early release a part to play.
explanation.walkthrough: PE, the school subject physical education, holds the other two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A parolee is a prisoner let out before the end of the sentence on condition of good behaviour.

clue.text: Alan's beginning to get increasingly wide. Nothing's consumed? That's increasingly wise

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, the only one kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the name

indicators.note: something consumed is used up and gone, so it is removed

parts.note: stouter means fatter, growing wider
nothing is zero, shaped like O; this letter is taken out

explanation.surface: Alan is starting to put on weight; if he eats nothing, that would be the wiser course.
explanation.walkthrough: The dieting story makes 'consumed' look like eating, but it signals that O vanishes from the word for fatter.
explanation.definitionFit: Astute means shrewd and perceptive, and the comparative form describes someone more so, cleverer than before.

clue.text: Songbirds steal in before onset of spring

parts.note: to rob is to steal
taken as written

indicators.note: the onset of a word is its start, so only the first letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the season

explanation.surface: Songbirds slip into the garden just before spring arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steal in' reads as creeping in quietly, but the two words give separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The robin, with its red breast, is a small European songbird, so the plural names several of them.

clue.text: Stacks by the German cranes

parts.note: der is the German masculine definite article
a rick is a stack of hay

explanation.surface: Stacks of hay stand next to the German's building cranes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' places the article beside the stacks; a rick is a large stack of hay or straw, a farm word.
explanation.definitionFit: A derrick is a kind of lifting crane with a pivoting arm, used on docks and oil rigs.
